names.name: nirguṇ bhakti / nirguṇ rām kī bhakti

definitions.definition: Love and remembrance directed to the formless Rām who is in every body, through the Name and the true guru, without images, avatāras or rites; the Lord is 'neither one nor two' and yet the Beloved.
Ravidās's devotion to the formless Lord as sandalwood to water, gold to bracelet.
Dādū's remembrance of the one stainless Rām of Hindu and Turk.

relations.note: The Sants love the nirguṇa as a person without accepting saguṇa forms as final; saguṇa bhaktas (e.g. Tulsīdās) reply that the two are not different.

name: Nirguṇa and saguṇa (the ultimate with and without qualities)

definitions.definition: The Sants place the nirguṇa above the saguṇa: stone images, pilgrimages and the avatāra (the son of Daśaratha) do not reach the secret of the Name.
Caraṇdās joins both: nirguṇa knowledge with devotion to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
The Lord is in every body as musk in the deer's navel, oil in sesame, fire in flint; he is 'in the breath of the breath', not in temple, mosque, Kaaba or Kailāsa.
Between you and me what difference? As gold and bracelet, water and wave.
The neighbour in the mirror-city, near yet a hundred thousand leagues away; the one who speaks but is not seen.

relations.note: The Sant 'Lord within' and the Bāul 'Man of the Heart' are the indwelling divine in two idioms (P3-path); the Bāuls stress the body and the living human, the Sants the Name.

name: The Man of the Heart (maner mānuṣ)

definitions.definition: The divine person dwelling in the human body — the unknown bird, the uncatchable Man, the neighbour in the mirror-city — longed for, sought through the guru and met in the body; worship of the human leads to becoming the golden human.

relations.note: Bāul and Sahajiyā names of the same indwelling Man.

definitions.definition: The divine present as the innate nature of human beings — Kṛṣṇa in the man, Rādhā in the woman; 'the truth of man is above all'.
The Master hidden in the human form, above all in the guru.
The natural Man whose worship in the human makes one golden.

name: The Kartā (Master) present in the human

definitions.definition: God is the one Kartā, present in Āulcānd (Caitanya returned) and in the living guru; he is worshipped alone, in the human, not in images.

name: The natural or innate (sahaja)

definitions.definition: The natural state in which the Lord is realized without forced yoga: eyes open, every act worship; Kabīr warns that everyone says 'sahaj' and no one knows it.
The innate beyond the two, known only by one who has crossed the darkness; the goal of the couple's discipline.
The sahaj path and the sahaj Man, found in the body under the guru.
The sahaja religion (satya-dharma) revealed by Āulcānd.

notes: The Buddhist Sahajiyā 'sahaja' of the siddhas (U44, same concept id expected) is the scholarly-hypothesized ancestor of the Bengali usage (brw:mahasiddha-to-vaisnava-sahajiya); the Sant usage comes via the Nāths (brw:natha-to-sant).

definitions.definition: Absorption that grows by the guru's grace without closing eyes or stopping ears: going about is circumambulation, work is service, lying down is prostration; the Lord's form is seen everywhere.

relations.note: Set by Kabīr against yogic absorption obtained by force (closing eyes, stopping ears, torturing the body).

name: The fourth state (cauthā pad) in Sant usage

definitions.definition: Beyond waking, dream and sleep and beyond the three qualities lies the 'fourth state' (cauthā pad, turīya), in which the Lord is known; Kabīr uses the Nāth-Vedāntic term.

relations.note: Same name as the Upaniṣadic fourth, used devotionally.

name: The inner regions of Sant Mat

definitions.definition: Above the eye centre (tīsrā til) the soul rises through Sahasdal Kanwal (thousand-petalled lotus; bell and conch), Trikuṭī (Brahm; drum/thunder), Daswān Dwār/Sunn and Mahāsunn (sārangī), Bhanwar Guphā (flute) and Sach Khand/Sat Lok (vīṇā), then Alakh, Agam and Anāmī/Radhasoami; the first two belong to Kāl's domain, the rest are purely spiritual.

notes: Beas-line presentation; the Agra texts differ in detail and numbering.

definitions.definition: The soul is surat, a drop of the ocean of the Supreme, a current of attention now scattered through the body and the senses; gathered at the eye centre it rises on the sound; with nirat (the seeing faculty) it hears and sees within.
The mind is the battlefield: restless elephant, thief, bird; defeat and victory are the mind's; the Name recited while it wanders is not remembrance; when it dies the Lord is found.
Sundardās: the mind is thief, monkey, mad elephant, tamed only by the guru's word and discrimination.
The mind is Kāl's agent, attached to the soul up to Trikuṭī; the soul must be freed from it by the sound current.
The mind addressed in every song ('o mind'), to be turned to truth and to the Man.
The Bījak's virtue of testing all doctrines, gods and practices as the mind's own products, as a jeweller tests gems; the discerning one (pārakhī) is not deceived by words.

name: The present and the inferred (bartamān and anumān)

definitions.definition: Knowledge is of the present, verifiable in the living body (bartamān); scripture, heaven and the gods of the books are inference and hearsay (anumān).
Kabīr's parallel stance: 'I speak of what I have seen with my eyes, you of what is written on paper'.

relations.note: Opposes reliance on scripture as a means of knowledge.

definitions.definition: The body is the true mosque and temple; service and worship are within (Dādū); the offering is body and mind (Ravidās).
The original Mecca is in this human body.
What is in the vessel is in the universe: the cosmos with its gods, rivers and pilgrimages is present in the body, which is therefore the field of search.
The eternal Vṛndāvana with its lakes and lotuses is within the body.

The body is a cage with eight rooms and nine doors and a mirror-palace above, where the unknown bird comes and goes; its currents, lotuses and 'moons' are known only through the guru; it is the only temple.
The body's inner lakes and lotuses as the abode of the divine couple.

name: The subtle body in Sant usage

definitions.definition: Nāth-derived anatomy: the three channels (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā, or Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī) meeting at trikuṭī, the six cakras, the tenth door, the sky-circle where nectar drips and the unstruck sound is heard; the body as a finely woven sheet.
Sundardās's yoga ullāsa sets out the cakras and the serpent power as a subordinate stage.
Six cakras below the eyes belong to the body (piṇḍ); the Sant practice starts at the eye centre and does not work through the lower cakras; above lie the regions.
The soul is covered by the physical, astral and causal bodies, which it leaves behind at the eye centre, Sahasdal Kanwal/Trikuṭī and Daswān Dwār respectively.
Kuṇḍalinī practice working up from the lower cakras is held to be unnecessary and hazardous; the Sants begin at the eye centre and rise by the sound.
Sundardās describes rousing the serpent power as part of yoga, below devotion and knowledge.

name: The body as the eternal Vṛndāvana

definitions.definition: The eternal Vṛndāvana, with its lakes and lotuses where Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa sport, is within the human body; the innate Man dwells there.

name: The inner lakes of the Sahajiyā body

definitions.definition: Sahajiyā manuals describe lakes (sarovara) in the body — of desire, of pride, of love and of the imperishable — through which the practitioner passes; recorded in outline only.

notes: Names and number of the lakes recalled with low confidence (Dimock's discussion); restricted context.

definitions.definition: A coded teaching on four bodily substances ('moons') whose secret handling under a guru belongs to Bāul body practice; the tradition insists it is secret and ruinous without a guru. RESTRICTED: no details recorded.
Practice goes upstream against the natural downward flow of desire and seed, as a fish swims against the tide; the one who goes with the current is lost. Doctrine only (restricted).
Kāma is reversed and refined into prema.

relations.note: The haṭha and Nāth idea of the upward-turned seed, in a devotional and couple-based frame; the Bāuls would not accept a purely yogic reading.

name: The qualities and the elements in Sant teaching

definitions.definition: Māyā binds with the noose of the three qualities (guṇa), from which the three gods arise; the body is woven of the five elements, which return to their source at death.
The three guṇas and five tattvas originate in the region of Brahm (Trikuṭī) and belong to Kāl's creation.

Māyā is the great swindler (mahāṭhaginī) who takes a different form in every house — Kamalā, Bhavānī, the idol, the pilgrim-water — and binds with the three qualities; at the origin 'one woman' from whom the gods came; often 'gold and woman'.

Truth above austerity; non-violence and a vegetarian diet (the goat eats leaves and is flayed); honest household labour and contentment (give only as much as my family needs); humility (none worse than I); keep the critic near; the sādhu known by conduct, not garb.
Erase the self, abandon the faults of body and mind, and be without enmity to all beings.
Low deeds, not birth, make a man low.
Four vows: lacto-vegetarian diet, no alcohol or drugs, a moral life, daily meditation.
Speak truth and walk the right path.
Caste has no standing before God: do not ask a sādhu's caste; the brahmin and the Turk came by the same way.
Ravidās names his Camār caste and its work without shame; the Lord raises the one whose touch the world calls polluting; in Begampura there is no second or third rank.
Lalon has never seen the form of caste; at birth and death no sign of it remains.
In the Kartā's fellowship there is one caste — while outward custom is kept in the world.
Ghāsīdās's Satnāmīs reject caste hierarchy and untouchability.
Balarām Hāḍi's followers reject brahmanical caste religion.
Hindu and Turk fight over Rām and Rahīm and neither knows the secret; the mullā shouts as if God were deaf, the paṇḍit worships stones; the one Lord is in every body.
Hindu and Muslim are two hands, two eyes of one body; the body is mosque and temple.
Temple and mosque block the path; rosary and tasbīh make no real difference.

name: Impartiality and the middle way (nipakh, madh)

definitions.definition: Dādū takes no side between Hindu and Turk and walks the middle between indulgence and harsh renunciation.
Idols, pilgrimage, ritual bathing, touch-purity, fasting and sacrifice, sectarian garb, the Veda and the Qur'ān recited without love are rejected; the yogī dyed his clothes, not his mind.
Every outward offering is already defiled (milk by the calf, flowers by the bee); purity is of the mind.
Your path is covered by temple and mosque.
'Among people, people's custom; with the true guru, oneness': the Kartābhajā keeps caste and religious custom outwardly while worshipping the Kartā alone within.

name: Women in the Sant and Bāul traditions

definitions.definition: The Sant verses often name woman with gold as māyā's snare (kanak-kāminī) and warn the renunciant against her; yet women Sants (Sahajobāī, Dayābāī; Mīrā is claimed as Ravidās's disciple) taught with authority, and Kabīr speaks as the bride of Rām.
Every woman is Rādhā in her svarūpa; the female partner is revered and may be the guru of the practice.
Satī Mā led the community and is venerated as the Mother.
The soul wanders through 8.4 million species; the human birth is the rare chance to remember the Name before Kāl grinds it between the mill-stones again.
The wheel of eighty-four under Kāl's law of karma, from which the initiate is freed.
The pot breaks and water merges with water; the one who has died while living cannot die; freedom is now, in sahaj.
The soul (haṃs) that has received the true Name passes Kāl and returns to Satlok, never to be reborn.
Begampura, the city without sorrow.
Return of the soul to Sach Khand and beyond to Anāmī, within at most four lives of initiation.

relations.note: The Sant jīvan-mṛtak and sahaj correspond to liberation while living; the Kabīr Panth and Sant Mat add a post-mortem return to Satlok/Sach Khand.

definitions.definition: The devotee who has let the self die while alive fears nothing and is served by Hari; the warrior who cuts off his own head wins the field; burn your own house and come with me.
Dying daily in meditation by withdrawing to the eye centre.
The love-practice of the one who has died while alive.

name: The three karmas in Sant Mat

definitions.definition: Pralabdh (destiny of this body) must be lived out; sinchit (stored) karma is taken over by the Master and burnt through practice; kriyaman (new) karma is avoided by living by the vows; the initiate is not reborn below the human form and returns home within four lives at most.
The liberated city of Ravidās: no grief, tax, fear, decline or ranks; citizens move freely; it is at once the state of the liberated and the ideal of a just order.
The true guru gives the one word that soaks every limb with love, opens infinite eyes, and is honoured before Govind because he showed Govind; his virtues cannot be written with the earth for paper.
The guru met in the unseen who placed his hand on Dādū's head.
Sahajobāī would give up Rām rather than forget the guru, who cut the round of birth that Hari gave.
The Sant Satguru embodies the highest region.
The guru is the means to God and is honoured above God for that reason (guru and Govind).
The guru is truth; the Kartā is present in the Mahāśay.

name: The necessity of a living master

definitions.definition: Only a living Sant Satguru can initiate, give the secret of the sound and guide and protect the soul within and at death; past masters cannot.
Kabīr promised a line of forty-two ācāryas through whom souls receive the Name, and warned of false teachers.

name: The guru in the Bāul path

definitions.definition: The Man is found only through the living guru (murśid, sāṃi); Bāuls take a dīkṣā-guru (initiation) and a śikṣā-guru (instruction in practice), and later the bhek (garb); the song itself is the guru's word, signed in his name; the teaching is secret and given only to the qualified.
Songs speak in double meanings (sandhyā-bhāṣā) of the body, the moons, the tide and the Man, so that practice is taught only to the initiated.
The manuals and padas conceal the practice in the language of Vaiṣṇava rasa.
The Bhāber Gīt is deliberately obscure, using the imagery of the bazaar and the company; the teaching is gupta.

relations.note: The Sant upside-down song and the Bengali coded song share the device of paradox that hides and reveals.

definitions.definition: Incarnations come from Kāl's regions to keep order in creation; Saints come from the highest region to take souls home and are above them.
Kabīr came in all four ages as the Sat Puruṣ's messenger; the three gods are Kāl's sons.
Kabīr is the supreme God above the gods of the three worlds.

name: The Sants on powers and miracles

definitions.definition: Riddhi and siddhi are māyā's snares; the yogī's feats and garb do not reach the Lord; the Sant seeks only the Name (the hagiographies nevertheless narrate miracles of protection, as signs of the Lord's care).
Inner experiences of light and sound are signposts, not the goal; the disciple is not to display or seek powers.
Separation is the sultan; the one who has it wakes and weeps while the world eats and sleeps; the arrow of separation is the Beloved's gift.
Longing for the Man of the Heart who comes near and cannot be held.

name: The Kabīr Panth cosmogony (Sat Puruṣ and Kāl Nirañjan)

definitions.definition: The Sat Puruṣ emanated sixteen sons; Nirañjan by austerity won the three worlds and Ādyā, begot Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś, and as Kāl binds souls; Kabīr comes in every age to lead souls back to Satlok.
Bījak: from light, sound and one woman came Hari, Brahmā and Tripurāri, and the world of forms.

relations.note: Inverts the Purāṇic account by making the creator a fallen power.

name: Kabīr's comings in the four ages

definitions.definition: Sat Sukṛt (Satya), Munīndra (Tretā), Karuṇāmay (Dvāpara), Kabīr (Kali).

name: Kāl and Dayāl (the negative and the merciful power)

definitions.definition: Creation below Daswān Dwār is ruled by Kāl, the negative power (universal mind), who administers karma and keeps souls in the three worlds; above is Dayāl, the merciful, whose Saints free souls.
Kāl Nirañjan against the Sat Puruṣ.

name: The grand divisions of creation (Sant Mat)

definitions.definition: Creation is in three (or four) grand divisions: piṇḍ (physical, the body), aṇḍ (astral), brahmāṇḍ (causal, to Trikuṭī/Daswān Dwār) — Kāl's domain — and above them the purely spiritual Dayāl Deś; spirit, spirit-and-mind, and mind-and-matter.

name: The bazaar of the soul (Kartābhajā imagery)

definitions.definition: The world is a bazaar where a new company has come; the soul is a trader, and the true merchandise is the Master's secret.
The Name (of Rām) remembered inwardly is the only raft; recited on beads while the mind wanders it is nothing; by the Name the Camār Ravidās is honoured by brahmins.
The Name is the Word within, not the spoken name.
The true Name given at initiation frees the soul from Kāl.
The guru's word awakens and the inner Word reveals: 'the Bījak shows the hidden wealth, the Word shows the soul'; at the origin were light and sound.
The Word is the audible life stream, the creative power that is also the way back.

relations.note: Both make sound/word the ultimate's own power; the Sant Word is heard within and is not the Veda (which Sant Mat places at Trikuṭī).

name: Union of the soul with the sound current (surat-śabd)

definitions.definition: The soul (surat) joins the sound current (śabd) at the eye centre and is drawn up by it through the regions to its source — the principle of surat-śabd yoga.

relations.note: Both teach absorption through successive inner sounds; the Sant Mat sounds are assigned to regions and the goal is beyond sound.

name: The five names and five sounds (Sant Mat)

definitions.definition: At initiation five names (of the lords of the five regions) are given for simran and kept confidential; each region has its sound — bell and conch, drum/thunder, sārangī, flute, vīṇā.

notes: The five names themselves are held confidential by the tradition and are not recorded.

definitions.definition: Riddling songs of impossible images (the lion grazing cows, the son born before the mother, the guru at the disciple's feet) that turn ordinary perception upside down; 'whoever understands this song is liberated'.
Sākhī (witness couplet), pad or śabd (song in a rāga), ramainī (doctrinal caupāī stanzas), arranged in aṅgas; sung in satsaṅg and bhajan.
The Bāul gān signed by the guru's and poet's names, sung with ektārā and dotārā; song is teaching, practice and code.

name: Death and dying in the Sant and Bāul traditions

definitions.definition: Death (kāl) stands over every head: do today what you would do tomorrow; the clay will knead the potter; between the mill-stones none survives; yet the death the world fears is joy to the devotee; Kabīr went to Maghar to die to refute the belief that dying in Kāśī liberates; he returned the sheet of the body unstained.
At death Kāl's messengers let pass the soul that bears the true Name and the pān-parvānā; the caukā rite is performed for the dead.
The Master himself receives the initiate at death; meditation is daily rehearsal of death.
The cage of green bamboo will break; if the neighbour touched me the torments of death would go; Bāuls and fakirs are commonly buried (samādhi) rather than cremated, as Lalon was at Cheuṛiyā.

notes: Bāul burial practice recorded from general report (moderate confidence).

name: Form, true form and superimposition (rūpa, svarūpa, āropa)

definitions.definition: Each person has an outer form (rūpa) and a divine true form (svarūpa) — Kṛṣṇa in the man, Rādhā in the woman; by āropa (superimposing svarūpa on rūpa) the partners' love becomes the love of the divine couple.

Kāma seeks one's own pleasure and prema the Beloved's (as the Caitanya-caritāmṛta says); the Sahajiyā holds that prema is refined out of kāma, not reached by suppressing it; the washerwoman's love had no trace of lust.

relations.note: Orthodox Gauḍīyas accept the same definitions but deny that prema can be reached by refining human kāma.

definitions.definition: The gopīs' love outside marriage is taken as the model of the practitioner's love for a partner (not the spouse), because it is selfless, risky and full of longing; recorded as doctrine only (restricted). The path is said to be hard as holding an elephant with a spider's thread.

relations.note: For the Gauḍīyas parakīyā belongs to Kṛṣṇa's līlā only and is never a human practice.

name: Caitanya as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body

definitions.definition: Caitanya is the union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body, and so the model of the sahaja union of the two principles in the human; the Gosvāmīs knew this esoteric meaning.
Caitanya returned as Āulcānd to reveal the sahaja religion.
The Gaṅgā is in the pure mind's bowl; the fish is thirsty in water while the Lord is in one's own house.
The original Mecca is the human body.
The Lord raises the lowly by his own mercy; Rām gives to all (Malūkdās); the guru's grace awakens sahaj.
Take me across, O merciful one — I have no boat or fare.

name: The Bāul–Fakir exchange (context)

definitions.definition: Hindu Bāuls and Muslim Fakirs share gurus, songs and practice: Lalon, a fakir with a Muslim guru, sings of Caitanya and of the Mecca in the body; the Fakirs use Sufi terms (murśid, mārephat, nūr) for the same path. Recorded as context only (Sufism is outside scope).

notes: Context only; U49 owns the Sant–Bāul–Sufi exchange.

definitions.definition: Nothing in me is mine; giving back to the Lord what is his costs nothing; saying 'you, you' the 'I' disappears.
Surrender to the Master's will (mauj) and acceptance of pralabdh karma as his gift.
The helpless prayer to be taken across by the merciful one.

name: The devotee as bride of the Lord (the bridal mood)

names.name: nihakarmī pativratā (the faithful wife without works) — an aṅga of the anthologies

definitions.definition: Kabīr sings as the bride whose husband, King Rām, has come home, with body as altar and mind as priest; the pain of separation (birah) is the bride's longing; the devotee as faithful wife (pativratā) of the one Lord.
The madhura mood realized in the human pair, each seeing the other's svarūpa as Rādhā or Kṛṣṇa (restricted context; doctrine only).
The lover longing for the Man of the Heart as for a beloved.

relations.note: Corresponds to the madhura (amorous) mood of the Gauḍīya rasa scheme; the Sants do not systematize moods.
